title: Πηνελόπης ἐνιπή
about: Amphinomus, who leads the suitors from Dulichium and pleases Penelope with his words, answers Antinous’s plan to kill Telemachus: killing one of royal stock is a dreadful thing, so they should first ask the will of Zeus, and if the gods forbid, stop. The suitors agree and go back to the house. Penelope, who has learned of the plot from the herald Medon, comes down with her women and stands in the doorway, veiled, to rebuke Antinous, reminding him how his father once fled to Odysseus for refuge when the people wanted him dead. Eurymachus soothes her with a promise that no man will touch Telemachus while he lives, and tells how Odysseus once fed him as a child, but the poet adds that he himself is preparing the young man’s destruction. Penelope weeps herself to sleep. At evening Eumaeus comes to the farm, where Athena has already made Odysseus look an old man again so that the swineherd will not know him; he tells Telemachus that he saw a ship full of armed men enter the harbour, and Telemachus smiles to his father in secret. They feast and go to bed.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes Antinous’s speech from the previous part. ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο ‘he spoke’, elided, with its τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of the οἱ that follows. οἱ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and they then’, where οἱ is a pronoun, not the article. ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ is a set phrase for a company struck quiet: ἀκήν is an adverb ‘hushed’ and the dative σιωπῇ ‘in silence’ says it again. The whole line stands word for word elsewhere in the poem, and its English here is the same.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀμφίνομος ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε,
Νίσου φαίδιμος υἱός, Ἀρητιάδαο ἄνακτος,
ὅς ῥ’ ἐκ Δουλιχίου πολυπύρου, ποιήεντος,
sentences.l:
To them Amphinomus addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them,
glorious son of Nisus, Aretes’ son, the lord,
who from Dulichium, rich-in-wheat, grassy,
sentences.i: Amphinomus addressed the assembly and spoke among them, the glorious son of Nisus, the lord, Aretes’ son, who came from Dulichium, rich in wheat and grassy,
sentences.n: ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε is ‘addressed the assembly and spoke among them’, the verb ἀγοράομαι ‘speak in assembly’ plus μετέειπε ‘spoke among’, a formula that introduces a speaker; the speech itself begins after line 399. τοῖσιν is ‘to them’, a pronoun in the dative plural. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is a stock epithet and is translated every time, here of υἱός ‘son’. Νίσου is a genitive, ‘of Nisus’, and ἄνακτος ‘the lord’ agrees with it; Ἀρητιάδαο is a second genitive agreeing with Νίσου, a patronymic in -αο, ‘Aretes’ son’. So Nisus is the lord, the son of an Aretes, and Amphinomus is Nisus’s son. The relative ὅς ῥ’ (ὅς ῥα) ‘who’ takes its verb in the next unit, ἡγεῖτο ‘was leading’. Δουλιχίου πολυπύρου is ‘Dulichium rich in wheat’, πολύπυρος being built on πολύς ‘much’ and πυρός ‘wheat’, and ποιήεντος ‘grassy’ is built on ποίη ‘grass’.

sentences.t:
ἡγεῖτο μνηστῆρσι, μάλιστα δὲ Πηνελοπείῃ
ἥνδανε μύθοισι·
sentences.l:
was leading the suitors, and most of all to Penelope
was he pleasing with his words;
sentences.i: and was the suitors’ leader, and pleased Penelope above all by what he said;
sentences.n: ἡγεῖτο μνηστῆρσι is ‘was leading the suitors’, ἡγέομαι taking the dative. The sentence runs on from the previous unit and stops here at Murray’s ano teleia, in the middle of line 398. μάλιστα δὲ Πηνελοπείῃ is ‘and most of all Penelope’, with a dative in -ῃ, and ἥνδανε ‘was pleasing to’ is the imperfect of ἁνδάνω, which takes a dative (Attic prose says ἀρέσκω); μύθοισι is a dative plural in -οισι, ‘by words’.

sentences.t: φρεσὶ γὰρ κέχρητ’ ἀγαθῇσιν·
sentences.l: for with wits good he was provided;
sentences.i: for he was furnished with good wits;
sentences.n: φρεσὶ γὰρ κέχρητ’ ἀγαθῇσιν is ‘for he is furnished with good wits’. κέχρητ’ is κέχρηται, the perfect of χράομαι ‘use’ (here ‘be provided with’), which takes the dative, here φρεσί ‘wits, mind’; ἀγαθῇσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν agreeing with it, ‘good’. The clause gives the reason why Amphinomus pleased Penelope.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐϋφρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: ὅ is ‘he’, a pronoun, and σφιν is ‘to them’, Homer’s short form of σφισιν. ἐϋφρονέων is the participle of ἐϋφρονέω ‘be well-minded’, built on ἐΰ ‘well’ and φρονέω ‘think’, and is kept as ‘well-disposed in mind’ in l and ‘with kindly intent’ in i. The rest of the line is the formula already met in 394: ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν, ‘addressed the assembly and spoke among them’, with the movable -ν. The speech begins on the next line.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, οὐκ ἂν ἐγώ γε κατακτείνειν ἐθέλοιμι
Τηλέμαχον·
sentences.l:
“O friends, not would I, for my part, to kill be willing
Telemachus;
sentences.i: “Friends, I for my part would not be willing to kill Telemachus;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι ‘O friends’ opens the speech; Amphinomus is speaking to the other suitors. οὐκ ἂν … ἐθέλοιμι is ‘I would not be willing’: ἄν with the optative gives a ‘would’, and ἐγώ γε adds ‘I for my part’. κατακτείνειν is the infinitive of κατακτείνω ‘kill’, and it comes before the verb it depends on, so the Greek says ‘to kill I would not be willing’. The unit ends at Murray’s ano teleia, in the middle of line 401.

sentences.t:
δεινὸν δὲ γένος βασιλήϊόν ἐστιν
κτείνειν·
sentences.l:
and dreadful is a kingly race
to kill;
sentences.i: and it is a dreadful thing to kill one of royal stock;
sentences.n: δεινὸν … ἐστιν κτείνειν is ‘it is dreadful to kill’, the infinitive κτείνειν saying what is dreadful. γένος βασιλήϊόν is ‘a royal stock, a family of kings’, the adjective βασιλήϊος ‘royal’ keeping the -ηϊ- that Attic βασίλειος has lost; Telemachus belongs to such a family. The unit ends at an ano teleia in the middle of line 402.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ πρῶτα θεῶν εἰρώμεθα βουλάς.
sentences.l: but first of the gods let us ask the plans.
sentences.i: but let us first inquire into the plans of the gods.
sentences.n: εἰρώμεθα is the subjunctive of εἴρομαι ‘ask, inquire’ (the Attic equivalent is ἐρέσθαι), used as an exhortation, ‘let us ask’. πρῶτα is the neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘first’, and θεῶν βουλάς is ‘the plans of the gods’, with βουλή ‘plan’ in its house sense.

sentences.t:
εἰ μέν κ’ αἰνήσωσι Διὸς μεγάλοιο θέμιστες,
αὐτός τε κτενέω τούς τ’ ἄλλους πάντας ἀνώξω·
sentences.l:
If indeed they should approve, the rules-of-right of great Zeus,
both I myself will kill and the others, all, I will urge on;
sentences.i: If the rules of right of great Zeus approve, I will kill him myself and urge all the others on;
sentences.n: εἰ … κ’ αἰνήσωσι is ‘if … should approve’: κε (here elided κ’) with the aorist subjunctive makes the condition, the same as Attic ἐάν, and the subject is Διὸς μεγάλοιο θέμιστες, ‘the rules of right of great Zeus’, a genitive in -οιο. κτενέω is the uncontracted future of κτείνω (Attic κτενῶ) and ἀνώξω the future of ἄνωγα ‘bid, urge’; the object of ‘kill’ is left unspoken, Telemachus. αὐτός τε … τούς τ’ ἄλλους πάντας is ‘both I myself … and all the others’, the two τε joining the clauses.

sentences.t: εἰ δέ κ’ ἀποτρωπῶσι θεοί, παύσασθαι ἄνωγα.
sentences.l: but if they turn it away, the gods, to stop I bid you.”
sentences.i: But if the gods turn it aside, I bid you stop.”
sentences.n: ἀποτρωπῶσι is the subjunctive of ἀποτρωπάω, a form of ἀποτρέπω ‘turn away’, and θεοί is its subject, ‘the gods’; the condition is again εἰ … κε with the subjunctive. ἄνωγα is a perfect with present sense, ‘I bid, I urge’, here with the infinitive παύσασθαι ‘to stop’ and the ‘you’ left unspoken. The closing quotation mark ends Amphinomus’s speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀμφίνομος, τοῖσιν δ’ ἐπιήνδανε μῦθος.
sentences.l: So spoke Amphinomus, and to them was pleasing the word.
sentences.i: So Amphinomus spoke, and his proposal pleased them.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀμφίνομος is ‘so spoke Amphinomus’, with ἔφατ’ the elided ἔφατο, here the speech-closing formula with a name in place of the pronoun. ἐπιήνδανε is ἐπί plus ἥνδανε, the imperfect of ἁνδάνω ‘please’ already seen in 398, and takes τοῖσιν ‘them’ in the dative; μῦθος is ‘word, proposal’.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀνστάντες ἔβαν δόμον εἰς Ὀδυσῆος,
ἐλθόντες δὲ καθῖζον ἐπὶ ξεστοῖσι θρόνοισιν.
sentences.l:
At once then, rising up, they went into the house of Odysseus,
and having come, they sat down upon polished chairs.
sentences.i: At once they rose and went into the house of Odysseus, and when they had come they sat down on polished chairs.
sentences.n: ἀνστάντες is the aorist participle of ἀνίστημι, ‘having risen’, with the Homeric ending -ντες; ἔβαν is the epic third-plural aorist of βαίνω ‘go’ (Attic ἔβησαν), ‘they went’, and δόμον εἰς is ‘into the house’. The first line repeats line 407 as it stands elsewhere in the poem, apart from its final stop, and the English reuses that wording. καθῖζον is the imperfect of καθίζω ‘sit down’, and ξεστοῖσι θρόνοισιν is a dative plural in -οισι, ‘on polished chairs’, ξεστός ‘smoothed, polished’.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια,
μνηστήρεσσι φανῆναι ὑπέρβιον ὕβριν ἔχουσι.
sentences.l:
But she, in turn, another thing thought of, circumspect Penelope,
to the suitors to show herself, holding exceeding insolence.
sentences.i: But circumspect Penelope had another thought: to show herself to the suitors, who were full of exceeding insolence.
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ αὖτ’ is ‘but she on her part’, the article-form ἡ being a pronoun. ἄλλ’ is the elided neuter of ἄλλος, ‘another thing’ (or, as ἄλλα, ‘other things’; the elision cannot say which), the object of ἐνόησε ‘thought of, had in mind’, and the infinitive φανῆναι, the aorist passive of φαίνω, gives what she thought of, ‘to appear, to show herself’. Πηνελόπεια is the Homeric form of the name, and περίφρων ‘circumspect’ is its stock epithet, translated every time. μνηστήρεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι. ὑπέρβιον ὕβριν ἔχουσι is ‘holding exceeding insolence’: ὑπέρβιος is ὑπέρ ‘beyond’ plus βίη ‘force’, ‘of excessive force’, and ὕβρις is ‘insolence’; the participle ἔχουσι is a dative plural agreeing with μνηστήρεσσι.

sentences.t: πεύθετο γὰρ οὗ παιδὸς ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ὄλεθρον·
sentences.l: for she was learning of her own child’s destruction in the halls;
sentences.i: for she had learned of her own son’s destruction in the halls;
sentences.n: πεύθετο is the imperfect of πεύθομαι, Homer’s form of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn by hearing’, with no augment. οὗ is the possessive ὅς, ‘her own’, in the masculine genitive singular agreeing with παιδός, so οὗ παιδός is ‘her own son’s’. ὄλεθρον ‘destruction’ is the object, and ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ‘in the halls’ is a dative plural in -οισιν with the older ἐνί for ἐν; the Greek leaves open whether ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν goes with πεύθετο or with ὄλεθρον, and the English leaves it open too.

sentences.t: κῆρυξ γάρ οἱ ἔειπε Μέδων, ὃς ἐπεύθετο βουλάς.
sentences.l: for the herald told her, Medon, who was learning the plans.
sentences.i: for the herald Medon had told her, who had learned their plans.
sentences.n: κῆρυξ … Μέδων is ‘the herald Medon’, set apart by the verb ἔειπε ‘told’, a past tense of the root of εἶπον; οἱ is ‘to her’. ὃς ἐπεύθετο βουλάς is ‘who was learning the plans’: ἐπεύθετο is the imperfect of πεύθομαι, now with its augment (compare πεύθετο in 411), and the plans are those of the suitors. The line says how Penelope knew.

sentences.t: βῆ δ’ ἰέναι μέγαρόνδε σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξίν.
sentences.l: She set out to go to the hall with attendant women.
sentences.i: She set off for the hall with her attendant women.
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἰέναι is ‘and she set out to go’: βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω, and with the infinitive ἰέναι of εἶμι ‘go’ it means ‘set off’. μέγαρόνδε is ‘to the hall’, with the suffix -δε that marks direction toward. σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξίν is ‘with attendant women’, a dative plural, the house rendering of the ἀμφίπολοι.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ μνηστῆρας ἀφίκετο δῖα γυναικῶν,
στῆ ῥα παρὰ σταθμὸν τέγεος πύκα ποιητοῖο,
ἄντα παρειάων σχομένη λιπαρὰ κρήδεμνα,
Ἀντίνοον δ’ ἐνένιπεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.l:
But when now to the suitors she came, heavenly-one of women,
she stood then beside the doorpost of the close-built roof,
before her cheeks holding her shining veil,
and Antinous she rebuked and spoke a word and called him by name:
sentences.i: But when she, heavenly among women, reached the suitors, she stood by the doorpost of the well-built hall, holding her shining veil before her cheeks, and rebuked Antinous, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: δῖα γυναικῶν is ‘heavenly-one of women’, the stock phrase for Penelope. The second and third lines, στῆ ῥα … λιπαρὰ κρήδεμνα, stand word for word in an earlier passage, and the English follows that. σταθμὸν τέγεος πύκα ποιητοῖο is ‘the doorpost of the close-built roof’, the roof being the hall’s; κρήδεμνα is a plural for the one veil, and ἄντα παρειάων ‘before her cheeks’ places it across her face. σχομένη is the aorist middle participle of ἔχω, ‘holding up’. Ἀντίνοον δ’ ἐνένιπεν is ‘and she rebuked Antinous’, ἐνένιπεν a past tense of ἐνίπτω ‘rebuke’; ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is the formula ‘spoke a word and called him by name’, with ἔκ … ὀνόμαζεν a tmesis for ἐξονομάζω. Penelope’s speech follows.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίνο’, ὕβριν ἔχων, κακομήχανε, καὶ δέ σέ φασιν
ἐν δήμῳ Ἰθάκης μεθ’ ὁμήλικας ἔμμεν ἄριστον
βουλῇ καὶ μύθοισι·
sentences.i: “Antinous, full of insolence, contriver of evil, and moreover they say that in the land of Ithaca you are the best of your own age in planning and in speech;
sentences.n: Ἀντίνο’ is the vocative Ἀντίνοε, elided. ὕβριν ἔχων ‘holding insolence’ is the phrase of 410 (there the dative plural ἔχουσι), now turned on Antinous himself, and κακομήχανε ‘contriver of evil’ is the vocative of κακομήχανος, built on κακός ‘bad’ and μηχανάομαι ‘devise’. καὶ δέ is ‘and moreover’, with φασιν ‘they say’ taking the accusative and infinitive σέ … ἔμμεν ἄριστον ‘that you are the best’, ἔμμεν being εἶναι. δήμῳ is ‘land’ in the house rendering, and μεθ’ ὁμήλικας is ‘among those of the same age’, μετά with the accusative. βουλῇ καὶ μύθοισι is ‘in plan and in speech’, ‘plan’ being βουλή’s house rendering; the unit stops at an ano teleia in the middle of line 420.

sentences.t: σὺ δ’ οὐκ ἄρα τοῖος ἔησθα.
sentences.l: but you were not, it seems, such a one.
sentences.i: but you were not, after all, that kind of man.
sentences.n: ἔησθα is ἦσθα ‘you were’, the imperfect of εἰμί with the older -ε-. ἄρα gives the sense of finding something out, ‘as it turns out’, and τοῖος is ‘of such a kind’, picking up the praise in the previous unit; with the imperfect, the speaker says what the facts now show.

sentences.l:
Madman, why do you for Telemachus both death and doom
stitch, and take no heed of suppliants, to whom indeed Zeus
is witness?
sentences.i: Madman, why do you contrive death and doom for Telemachus, and take no heed of suppliants, whose witness is Zeus?
sentences.n: μάργε is the vocative of μάργος, ‘raging, frenzied’, an insult. τίη is Homer’s form of τί ‘why’, and ῥάπτεις is ‘you stitch’, a figure for devising a scheme (the same image as in κακορραφίη ‘ill-contriving’); with it θάνατόν τε μόρον τε ‘both death and doom’ names what is stitched for Telemachus, and the present tense says that it is under way. ἐμπάζεαι is ἐμπάζῃ, ‘you take heed of’, with its -εαι ending left uncontracted and the object ἱκέτας ‘suppliants’. οἷσιν is ‘to whom’, and Ζεὺς μάρτυρος leaves ‘is’ unspoken; μάρτυρος stands where the usual form is μάρτυς ‘witness’, and the form is an unusual one. The unit ends at the question mark in the middle of line 423.

sentences.t: οὐδ’ ὁσίη κακὰ ῥάπτειν ἀλλήλοισιν.
sentences.l: nor is it holy evils to stitch for one another.
sentences.i: It is not right to contrive evils against one another.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὁσίη has ἐστί ‘is’ understood, ‘nor is it right’: ὁσίη is the feminine of ὅσιος ‘sanctioned by divine law’, and the infinitive κακὰ ῥάπτειν says what is not so sanctioned. κακὰ ῥάπτειν ‘to stitch evils’ repeats the image of ῥάπτεις in the line before, and ἀλλήλοισιν is a dative plural, ‘for one another’.

sentences.t:
ἦ οὐκ οἶσθ’ ὅτε δεῦρο πατὴρ τεὸς ἵκετο φεύγων,
δῆμον ὑποδείσας;
sentences.l:
Do you not indeed know when hither your father came fleeing,
having feared the people?
sentences.i: Do you not know when your father came here in flight, in fear of the people?
sentences.n: ἦ οὐκ introduces a question that expects ‘yes’, ‘do you not know?’, and οἶσθ’ is οἶσθα ‘you know’, taking a clause with ὅτε ‘when’. τεός is Ionic for σός ‘your’, ἵκετο is the unaugmented aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘come’, and φεύγων ‘fleeing’ is a present participle. ὑποδείσας is the aorist participle of ὑποδείδω ‘shrink in fear before’, with δῆμον ‘people’ as its object; here the people of the land, not the land itself. The unit ends at the question mark in the middle of line 425.

sentences.t:
δὴ γὰρ κεχολώατο λίην,
οὕνεκα ληϊστῆρσιν ἐπισπόμενος Ταφίοισιν
ἤκαχε Θεσπρωτούς·
sentences.i: for they were exceedingly angry, because he had joined the Taphian raiders and brought grief on the Thesprotians;
sentences.n: κεχολώατο is the pluperfect middle of χολόομαι ‘be angry’, with the ending -ατο for -ντο, ‘they had become angry, they were angry’, and λίην is ‘exceedingly’. οὕνεκα is ‘because’, ἐπισπόμενος the aorist middle participle of ἐφέπομαι ‘follow, join’, taking the dative ληϊστῆρσιν … Ταφίοισιν ‘Taphian raiders’. ἤκαχε is the aorist of ἀκαχίζω ‘distress, grieve’; the Greek says only that he ‘grieved’ the Thesprotians, and it is taken here of the harm of raiding them. The unit stops at an ano teleia in the middle of line 427.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἡμῖν ἄρθμιοι ἦσαν·
sentences.l: and they to us were friendly;
sentences.i: and they were on friendly terms with us;
sentences.n: οἱ is ‘they’, a pronoun, the Thesprotians, and ἡμῖν is ‘to us’, the Ithacans. ἄρθμιοι is a plural of ἄρθμιος ‘friendly, bound together’, built on the root of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, and the verb is ἦσαν ‘were’.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥ’ ἔθελον φθῖσαι καὶ ἀπορραῖσαι φίλον ἦτορ
ἠδὲ κατὰ ζωὴν φαγέειν μενοεικέα πολλήν·
sentences.l:
him they wished to destroy and to tear away his dear heart
and to devour his living, satisfying, abundant;
sentences.i: They wished to destroy him and tear the life from him, and to devour his abundant, satisfying living;
sentences.n: τόν ῥ’ is τὸν ῥα, ‘him’, the pronoun, Antinous’s father. ἔθελον is ‘they wished’, with no augment; φθῖσαι and ἀπορραῖσαι are aorist infinitives of φθίω ‘destroy’ and ἀπορραίω ‘tear away’, and φίλον ἦτορ ‘dear heart’ is what is torn out, meaning his life. κατὰ … φαγέειν is tmesis for κατεσθίω ‘devour’, with φαγέειν the uncontracted infinitive (Attic φαγεῖν); ζωὴν is here ‘living’, the means of life, not ‘life’ itself, and μενοεικέα ‘satisfying’ and πολλήν ‘abundant’ both agree with it.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ Ὀδυσεὺς κατέρυκε καὶ ἔσχεθεν ἱεμένους περ.
sentences.l: But Odysseus held them back and restrained them, eager though they were.
sentences.i: But Odysseus held them back and checked them, eager as they were.
sentences.n: κατέρυκε is ‘held back’, from κατερύκω, and ἔσχεθεν is a third-singular aorist of ἔχω with the epic by-form ending -θε(ν), ‘checked, restrained’. ἱεμένους περ is ‘eager though they were’, the participle of ἵημι with concessive περ; the object of both verbs is the unspoken ‘them’.

sentences.t:
τοῦ νῦν οἶκον ἄτιμον ἔδεις, μνάᾳ δὲ γυναῖκα
παῖδά τ’ ἀποκτείνεις, ἐμὲ δὲ μεγάλως ἀκαχίζεις·
sentences.l:
His house now dishonoured you devour, and you woo his wife
and his child you seek to kill, and me greatly you grieve;
sentences.i: Now you eat up his dishonoured house, and court his wife, and try to kill his child, and cause me great grief;
sentences.n: τοῦ is ‘his’, the genitive of the demonstrative pronoun, standing for Odysseus; it is not the possessive ὅς. οἶκον ἄτιμον is ‘a dishonoured house’, ἄτιμος ‘without honour’. ἔδεις is ‘you eat’ and μνάᾳ ‘you woo’, the second singular of μνάομαι, taking the accusative γυναῖκα. ἀποκτείνεις is a present tense, and it is rendered ‘seek to kill’ because the killing has not been done. ἀκαχίζεις ‘you distress’ is the verb of ἤκαχε in 427, and μεγάλως is ‘greatly’. The unit ends at an ano teleia, closing the line.

sentences.t: ἀλλά σε παύσασθαι κέλομαι καὶ ἀνωγέμεν ἄλλους.
sentences.l: But you to stop I bid, and to bid the others.”
sentences.i: But I bid you stop, and bid the others do so too.”
sentences.n: κέλομαι is ‘I bid’, and παύσασθαι ‘to stop’ is an aorist middle infinitive; ἀνωγέμεν is the infinitive of ἄνωγα ‘bid’ in -έμεν, with ἄλλους ‘the others’ as its object. The line asks Antinous to stop and to tell the other suitors to stop. The closing quotation mark ends Penelope’s speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτ’ Εὐρύμαχος, Πολύβου πάϊς, ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: Her then in turn spoke Eurymachus, Polybus’ son, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Eurymachus, son of Polybus, spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘her’, Penelope; the forms that look like the article are pronouns in Homer. αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’, and πάϊς is the Homeric form of παῖς ‘son’, so Πολύβου πάϊς is ‘son of Polybus’. ἀντίον ηὔδα is ‘spoke face to face’, and the line as a whole is a fixed formula that introduces a reply.

sentences.t:
κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο, περίφρον Πηνελόπεια,
θάρσει·
sentences.l:
“Daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope,
take courage;
sentences.i: “Daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope, take courage;
sentences.n: κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο is ‘daughter of Icarius’, the genitive in -οιο, and the vocative περίφρον Πηνελόπεια repeats the stock epithet from 409, ‘circumspect’. θάρσει is the imperative of θαρσέω ‘take courage’. The unit stops at an ano teleia in the middle of line 436.

sentences.t: μή τοι ταῦτα μετὰ φρεσὶ σῇσι μελόντων.
sentences.l: let not these things be a care to you in your mind.
sentences.i: do not let these things weigh on your mind.
sentences.n: μελόντων is a third plural imperative of μέλω ‘be a care to’, ‘let them be’, and μή makes it ‘let them not be’; τοι is ‘to you’ (σοι). μετὰ φρεσὶ σῇσι is ‘in your mind’, the dative plural of φρήν with the feminine dative plural σῇσι ‘your’. The sense of this half-line stands in an earlier passage and the English is the same.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἔσθ’ οὗτος ἀνὴρ οὐδ’ ἔσσεται οὐδὲ γένηται,
ὅς κεν Τηλεμάχῳ σῷ υἱέϊ χεῖρας ἐποίσει
ζώοντός γ’ ἐμέθεν καὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ δερκομένοιο.
sentences.l:
There is not this man, nor will be, nor may come to be,
who on Telemachus, your son, hands will lay,
while I live, and upon the earth am looking.
sentences.i: There is no man, nor will there be, nor can there ever come to be one, who will lay hands on Telemachus, your son, while I live and look upon the earth.
sentences.n: οὐκ ἔσθ’ is οὐκ ἔστι ‘there is not’, ἔσσεται is the future ‘will be’ with doubled σ, and γένηται is the aorist subjunctive ‘may come to be’. ἀνήρ ‘man’ is the thing there is none of, and οὗτος ‘this’ points to the man the clause defines. ὅς κεν … ἐποίσει is ‘who shall lay’, the future of ἐπιφέρω, with χεῖρας ‘hands’ as its object; Τηλεμάχῳ σῷ υἱέϊ is a dative, ‘on Telemachus, your son’. ζώοντός γ’ ἐμέθεν is ‘while I am alive’, a genitive with the participle, ἐμέθεν being Homer’s ἐμοῦ, and καὶ … δερκομένοιο adds ‘and looking’ (the participle of δέρκομαι ‘see’) ‘on the earth’.

sentences.t: ὧδε γὰρ ἐξερέω, καὶ μὴν τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
sentences.l: for thus I will declare, and truly accomplished it will be;
sentences.i: For this I will declare, and it will surely be accomplished:
sentences.n: ὧδε is ‘thus’, pointing to what follows. ἐξερέω is ‘I will speak out’, a future from the root of εἶπον, καὶ μὴν ‘and truly’, and τετελεσμένον ἔσται is a perfect participle with ‘will be’, ‘it will be a thing accomplished’, from τελέω ‘bring to pass’. The unit ends at Murray’s ano teleia at the end of the line.

sentences.t:
αἶψά οἱ αἷμα κελαινὸν ἐρωήσει περὶ δουρὶ
ἡμετέρῳ, ἐπεὶ ἦ καὶ ἐμὲ πτολίπορθος Ὀδυσσεὺς
πολλάκι γούνασιν οἷσιν ἐφεσσάμενος κρέας ὀπτὸν
ἐν χείρεσσιν ἔθηκεν, ἐπέσχε τε οἶνον ἐρυθρόν.
sentences.l:
Quickly his blood, dark, will gush around our
spear, since indeed me also the city-sacking Odysseus
often upon his own knees having set, roast meat
in my hands put, and held out red wine.
sentences.i: Quickly his dark blood will gush about our spear, for Odysseus, the city-sacker, often set me on his own knees, put roast meat in my hands, and held out red wine to me.
sentences.n: αἶψά οἱ αἷμα κελαινόν is ‘quickly for him the dark blood’, οἱ being a dative of the person whose blood it is, and ἐρωήσει the future of ἐρωέω ‘gush, rush’. περὶ δουρὶ ἡμετέρῳ is ‘around our spear’, with περί the preverb-like preposition and δουρί the dative of δόρυ. ἐπεὶ ἦ καὶ ἐμέ is ‘since truly me also’, and πτολίπορθος ‘city-sacker’ (built on πτολίεθρον ‘city’ and πέρθω ‘sack’) is Odysseus’s epithet. ἐφεσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐφέζω ‘set upon’, here causative, ‘having set me’; γούνασιν οἷσιν is ‘on his own knees’, with οἷσιν the possessive ὅς, ‘his own’. κρέας ὀπτόν is ‘roast meat’, and ἐπέσχε τε οἶνον ἐρυθρόν is ‘and held out red wine’. The sentence runs four lines to Murray’s full stop.

sentences.t:
τῷ μοι Τηλέμαχος πάντων πολὺ φίλτατός ἐστιν
ἀνδρῶν, οὐδέ τί μιν θάνατον τρομέεσθαι ἄνωγα
ἔκ γε μνηστήρων·
sentences.i: That is why Telemachus is by far the dearest of all men to me, and I do not at all bid him fear death from the suitors;
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘for that reason’, the dative of the demonstrative used as an adverb. πάντων … ἀνδρῶν ‘of all men’ is split around the verb, πολύ ‘by far’ strengthening φίλτατος ‘dearest’. οὐδέ τί μιν … ἄνωγα is ‘and I do not at all bid him’, the negative going with ἄνωγα and so with the infinitive τρομέεσθαι ‘to fear’, the uncontracted infinitive of τρομέω ‘tremble before’. ἔκ γε μνηστήρων is ‘from the suitors, at least’. The unit stops at an ano teleia in the middle of line 447.

sentences.t: θεόθεν δ’ οὐκ ἔστ’ ἀλέασθαι.
sentences.l: but from the gods it is not possible to escape.”
sentences.i: but what comes from the gods cannot be escaped.”
sentences.n: θεόθεν is ‘from the gods’, the suffix -θεν marking the source, and οὐκ ἔστ’ is οὐκ ἔστι ‘it is not possible’, with ἀλέασθαι the aorist infinitive of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid, escape’. The closing quotation mark ends Eurymachus’s speech.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο θαρσύνων, τῷ δ’ ἤρτυεν αὐτὸς ὄλεθρον.
sentences.l: So he spoke, encouraging her, but for him prepared he himself destruction.
sentences.i: So he spoke, to reassure her, though he himself was preparing destruction for him.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’, φάτο being the unaugmented ἔφατο, and θαρσύνων ‘encouraging’ is the participle of θαρσύνω ‘make bold’, here ‘reassuring’ Penelope. τῷ is ‘for him’, Telemachus, and ἤρτυεν is the imperfect of ἀρτύω ‘prepare, arrange’, so αὐτός ‘he himself’ and ὄλεθρον ‘destruction’ show Eurymachus preparing the very harm he has just sworn to prevent; the narrator’s remark gives away that the oath is false.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ εἰσαναβᾶσ’ ὑπερώϊα σιγαλόεντα
κλαῖεν ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆα, φίλον πόσιν, ὄφρα οἱ ὕπνον
ἡδὺν ἐπὶ βλεφάροισι βάλε γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l:
She then, having gone up to the upper rooms, glossy,
wept then for Odysseus, her dear husband, until upon her sleep,
sweet, upon her eyelids cast gleaming-eyed Athena.
sentences.i: She went up to her glossy upper rooms and wept then for Odysseus, her dear husband, until gleaming-eyed Athena cast sweet sleep upon her eyelids.
sentences.n: ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ is ‘she then’, ἡ the pronoun; εἰσαναβᾶσ’ is the aorist participle of εἰσαναβαίνω ‘go up into’, and ὑπερώϊα σιγαλόεντα is ‘the glossy upper rooms’, the plural ὑπερώϊα being the upper storey, σιγαλόεις ‘glossy’. The next two lines repeat an earlier passage of the poem, so the English of ‘she wept then … sleep upon her eyelids’ is the same. κλαῖεν is the imperfect of κλαίω, without augment, and ὄφρα means ‘until’ here; βάλε is the unaugmented aorist ‘cast’, and ἡδὺν ‘sweet’ goes with ὕπνον ‘sleep’. γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη is ‘gleaming-eyed Athena’; what γλαυκῶπις exactly means is a matter of dispute.

sentences.t:
ἑσπέριος δ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ καὶ υἱέϊ δῖος ὑφορβὸς
ἤλυθεν·
sentences.l:
And at evening to Odysseus and his son the heavenly swineherd
came;
sentences.i: In the evening the heavenly swineherd came to Odysseus and his son;
sentences.n: ἑσπέριος is an adjective used as an adverb, ‘at evening’. Ὀδυσῆϊ καὶ υἱέϊ is a dative, ‘to Odysseus and his son’, the son being Telemachus, and δῖος ὑφορβός is ‘the heavenly swineherd’, with the stock epithet translated each time. ἤλυθεν is a Homeric past tense of ἔρχομαι, Attic ἦλθεν. The unit stops at an ano teleia in the middle of line 453.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἄρα δόρπον ἐπισταδὸν ὡπλίζοντο,
σῦν ἱερεύσαντες ἐνιαύσιον.
sentences.l:
and they then supper standing-by were preparing,
having slaughtered a pig a year old.
sentences.i: and they were getting supper ready, standing by, having slaughtered a year-old pig.
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and they then’, the pronoun οἱ being Odysseus and Telemachus. δόρπον ‘supper’ is the evening meal. ἐπισταδόν is an adverb built on ἐφίστημι ‘stand by’, ‘standing by’, and ὡπλίζοντο is the imperfect of ὁπλίζω ‘make ready’. ἱερεύσαντες is ‘having slaughtered’, the aorist participle of ἱερεύω, and ἐνιαύσιον ‘a year old’ agrees with σῦν ‘pig’. The unit ends at a full stop in the middle of line 454.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀθήνη,
ἄγχι παρισταμένη, Λαερτιάδην Ὀδυσῆα
ῥάβδῳ πεπληγυῖα πάλιν ποίησε γέροντα,
sentences.l:
But Athena,
close by, standing near, the son of Laertes, Odysseus,
with her wand having struck, again made an old man,
sentences.i: But Athena, standing close beside him, struck Odysseus, son of Laertes, with her wand and made him an old man again,
sentences.n: παρισταμένη is the present middle participle of παρίστημι, ‘standing near’, and ἄγχι is ‘close by’. Λαερτιάδην Ὀδυσῆα is ‘Odysseus, son of Laertes’, a patronymic in apposition. πεπληγυῖα is a perfect participle of πλήσσω ‘strike’, used here as ‘having struck’, and ῥάβδῳ is ‘with a wand’; πάλιν ποίησε γέροντα is ‘made an old man again’, ποίησε having dropped its augment. The sentence runs on and is cut here at a comma, since it would run past four lines.

sentences.t:
λυγρὰ δὲ εἵματα ἕσσε περὶ χροΐ, μή ἑ συβώτης
γνοίη ἐσάντα ἰδὼν καὶ ἐχέφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ
ἔλθοι ἀπαγγέλλων μηδὲ φρεσὶν εἰρύσσαιτο.
sentences.l:
and grievous clothes she put on his skin, lest him the swineherd
should know, seeing him face to face, and to sound-minded Penelope
come reporting, nor keep it in his mind.
sentences.i: and put grievous clothes on his body, so that the swineherd would not recognise him on seeing him face to face, and go to sound-minded Penelope with the report, or keep it in his own mind.
sentences.n: λυγρὰ … εἵματα is ‘grievous clothes’, and ἕσσε is the aorist of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’, ‘she put on him’, with περὶ χροΐ ‘around his skin’. μή ἑ … γνοίη is ‘lest he should know him’: μή with the optative states what is to be avoided, ἑ is ‘him’, and ἐσάντα is ‘face to face’. συβώτης ‘swineherd’ is the subject. ἐχέφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ is ‘sound-minded Penelope’ in the dative, ἐχέφρων ‘sound-minded’ being a different stock epithet from the περίφρων of 409, kept apart from it. ἔλθοι ἀπαγγέλλων is ‘should go reporting’, and μηδὲ φρεσὶν εἰρύσσαιτο is ‘nor keep it in his mind’, εἰρύσσαιτο being the aorist middle optative of ἐρύομαι ‘guard, keep’.

sentences.t: τὸν καὶ Τηλέμαχος πρότερος πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.l: Him also Telemachus, first, with a word addressed:
sentences.i: Telemachus spoke to him first, with these words:
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’, the swineherd, a pronoun. πρὸς … ἔειπεν is a tmesis, a split form of προσεῖπε ‘spoke to, addressed’, with ἔειπεν the aorist of the root of εἶπον, and μῦθον ‘a speech’ stands between the two halves. πρότερος ‘first’ is an adjective used as an adverb, and καί is ‘also’; with πρότερος it says that Telemachus was the first to speak.

sentences.t: ἦλθες, δῖ’ Εὔμαιε.
sentences.l: “You have come, heavenly Eumaeus.
sentences.i: “You have come, heavenly Eumaeus.
sentences.n: ἦλθες ‘you came’ is an aorist with the force of ‘you have come’, a greeting. δῖ’ is δῖε, the vocative of δῖος, and is translated ‘heavenly’, the same as at 452. Εὔμαιε is the vocative of Εὔμαιος ‘Eumaeus’, the swineherd’s name.

sentences.t: τί δὴ κλέος ἔστ’ ἀνὰ ἄστυ;
sentences.l: What now is the report up through the town?
sentences.i: What is being said throughout the town?
sentences.n: τί δή is ‘what, then’ and ἔστ’ is ἔστι ‘is’. κλέος is properly ‘what is heard, report’, the word that can also mean ‘fame’; here it is the talk of the town. ἀνὰ ἄστυ is ‘up and down the town’, ἀνά with the accusative. The unit ends at the question mark that closes line 461.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥ’ ἤδη μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες ἔνδον ἔασιν
ἐκ λόχου, ἦ ἔτι μ’ αὖτ’ εἰρύαται οἴκαδ’ ἰόντα;
sentences.l:
Surely already the lordly suitors within are
from the ambush, or still me in turn they watch for as I go homeward?”
sentences.i: Are the lordly suitors already back inside, out of their ambush, or are they still watching for me as I head home?”
sentences.n: ἦ ῥ’ is the question particle ἦ with ῥα, ‘is it so that’, not the speech-closing ἦ ῥα ‘he spoke’. μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες is ‘the lordly suitors’, and ἔνδον ἔασιν is ‘are within’, ἔασιν being Homer’s εἰσίν; ἐκ λόχου is ‘from the ambush’, said of the men who have come away from it. ἦ ἔτι … εἰρύαται is ‘or are they still watching for’, εἰρύαται being a present of ἐρύομαι ‘guard, watch for’ with the old ending -αται, and μ’ αὖτ’ is ‘me in turn’. οἴκαδ’ ἰόντα is ‘going homeward’, the accusative participle agreeing with μ’. The closing quotation mark ends Telemachus’s question.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.l: Him, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: τὸν … προσέφης is the second-person form of the reply-formula: Homer turns from the story to speak to Eumaeus directly, ‘you addressed’, with ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ and Εὔμαιε συβῶτα as the vocative ‘Eumaeus the swineherd’. The line stands word for word elsewhere in the poem, and its English is the same.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἔμελέν μοι ταῦτα μεταλλῆσαι καὶ ἐρέσθαι
ἄστυ καταβλώσκοντα·
sentences.l:
“Not was it a care to me these things to inquire into and to ask,
going down to the town;
sentences.i: “I was not concerned to inquire into these things and ask about them as I went down to the town;
sentences.n: οὐκ ἔμελέν μοι is ‘it was not a care to me’, with ἔμελεν in its imperfect, and the two infinitives μεταλλῆσαι ‘to inquire into’ and ἐρέσθαι ‘to ask’ say what he did not care to do; ταῦτα ‘these things’ is the object. ἄστυ καταβλώσκοντα is ‘going down to the town’, the accusative participle of καταβλώσκω agreeing with the unspoken ‘me’. The unit stops at an ano teleia in the middle of line 466.

sentences.t:
τάχιστά με θυμὸς ἀνώγει
ἀγγελίην εἰπόντα πάλιν δεῦρ’ ἀπονέεσθαι.
sentences.l:
very quickly me my heart bade
news having told back here to return.
sentences.i: my heart urged me to return here again as quickly as possible, once I had told my news.
sentences.n: τάχιστα is the superlative adverb ‘as quickly as possible’, and με θυμὸς ἀνώγει is ‘my heart urged me’, ἀνώγει being the imperfect of ἄνωγα ‘bid’ and θυμός ‘heart’. ἀγγελίην εἰπόντα is ‘having told the news’, an accusative participle agreeing with με, and ἀπονέεσθαι is the infinitive of ἀπονέομαι ‘go back’.

sentences.t:
ὡμήρησε δέ μοι παρ’ ἑταίρων ἄγγελος ὠκύς,
κῆρυξ, ὃς δὴ πρῶτος ἔπος σῇ μητρὶ ἔειπεν.
sentences.l:
But there met me, from the companions, a messenger, swift,
a herald, who indeed first a word to your mother told.
sentences.i: But a swift messenger from your companions fell in with me, a herald, who was the first to give your mother the word.
sentences.n: ὡμήρησε is ‘met, fell in with’, from the rare verb ὁμηρέω, whose sense is taken from context; μοι is ‘me’. παρ’ ἑταίρων is ‘from the companions’, the Greek giving no ‘your’; they are Telemachus’s crew, hence ‘your companions’ in i, and ἄγγελος ὠκύς is ‘a swift messenger’, with ὠκύς translated ‘swift’ every time. κῆρυξ ‘herald’ explains ἄγγελος. ὃς δὴ πρῶτος ἔπος σῇ μητρὶ ἔειπεν is ‘who first told your mother the word’; ἔπος ‘word’ is the news, and σῇ is ‘your’.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι τό γε οἶδα·
sentences.l: But another thing, mark you, that I know;
sentences.i: But there is something else that I do know;
sentences.n: ἄλλο δέ τοι τό γε οἶδα is ‘but another thing, I tell you, this I know’. τοι is either ‘to you’ or the particle ‘mark you’; τό γε points to the thing that comes next. οἶδα is ‘I know’. The unit ends at an ano teleia in the middle of line 470.

sentences.t: τὸ γὰρ ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσιν.
sentences.l: for it I saw with my eyes.
sentences.i: for I saw it with my own eyes.
sentences.n: ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω ‘I saw’, with the object τὸ ‘it’, and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, ‘with the eyes’. The γάρ gives the reason he can say he knows.

sentences.t:
ἤδη ὑπὲρ πόλιος, ὅθι θ’ Ἕρμαιος λόφος ἐστίν,
ἦα κιών, ὅτε νῆα θοὴν ἰδόμην κατιοῦσαν
ἐς λιμέν’ ἡμέτερον·
sentences.i: I was already above the city, where the hill of Hermes stands, when, as I went, I saw a swift ship coming into our harbour;
sentences.n: ὑπὲρ πόλιος is ‘above the city’, with the genitive of πόλις. Ἕρμαιος λόφος is ‘the hill of Hermes’, Ἕρμαιος ‘of Hermes’, a hill above the city; the passage says no more of it. ἦα is ‘I was going’, the imperfect of εἶμι, and κιών the participle of κίω ‘go’. νῆα θοήν is ‘a swift ship’, with νῆα the accusative of νηῦς and θοός ‘swift’; ἰδόμην is the aorist middle ‘I caught sight of’. κατιοῦσαν ‘coming down’ agrees with νῆα, and ἐς λιμέν’ ἡμέτερον is ‘into our harbour’, λιμέν’ being λιμένα. The unit ends at an ano teleia in the middle of line 473.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ δ’ ἔσαν ἄνδρες ἐν αὐτῇ,
βεβρίθει δὲ σάκεσσι καὶ ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοισι·
sentences.l:
and many were the men in her,
and she was heavy with shields and spears double-pointed;
sentences.i: and there were many men in her, and she was weighed down with shields and double-pointed spears;
sentences.n: ἔσαν is ἦσαν ‘were’. βεβρίθει is a pluperfect of βρίθω ‘be heavy’, used as ‘was laden’, and σάκεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι of σάκος ‘shield’. ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοισι is ‘spears’ with an epithet whose meaning is not known: ἀμφιγύοισι is usually guessed to mean ‘pointed at both ends’, and ‘double-pointed’ is a guess taken from that. The unit ends at an ano teleia closing the line.

sentences.t: καὶ σφέας ὠΐσθην τοὺς ἔμμεναι, οὐδέ τι οἶδα.
sentences.l: and them I supposed those to be, but nothing do I know.”
sentences.i: and I supposed them to be those men, but I know nothing of it.”
sentences.n: σφέας is ‘them’, the accusative of the pronoun, and ὠΐσθην is the aorist passive of ὀΐομαι ‘suppose’, ‘I supposed’. τοὺς is ‘those’, a demonstrative, and ἔμμεναι is ‘to be’. οὐδέ τι οἶδα is ‘and I know nothing’, said of what the crew really are. The closing quotation mark ends Eumaeus’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, μείδησεν δ’ ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο
ἐς πατέρ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἰδών, ἀλέεινε δ’ ὑφορβόν.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and smiled the sacred force of Telemachus,
at his father with his eyes looking, but he avoided the swineherd.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the strong, sacred figure of Telemachus smiled, looking at his father with his eyes, but he avoided the swineherd.
sentences.n: ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο, literally ‘the sacred force of Telemachus’, is a periphrasis for the person, used in place of the bare name and translated the same way each time. μείδησεν is the aorist of μειδάω ‘smile’. ἐς πατέρ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἰδών is ‘looking at his father with his eyes’, and ἀλέεινε δ’ ὑφορβόν is ‘but he avoided the swineherd’, the δέ setting the swineherd against the father: the Greek says only that he avoided him, and the smile went to his father.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν παύσαντο πόνου τετύκοντό τε δαῖτα,
δαίνυντ’, οὐδέ τι θυμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐΐσης.
sentences.l:
And they, when then they had ceased from toil and had made ready the feast,
feasted, and not at all did the heart lack the equal feast.
sentences.i: And when they had ended their labour and prepared the meal, they feasted, and their hearts went short of nothing in the equally shared feast.
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν is ‘and when, then, they’; παύσαντο πόνου is ‘ceased from toil’, with the genitive, and τετύκοντο is the aorist middle of τεύχω ‘make ready’, with δαῖτα ‘a feast’ as its object. δαίνυντ’ is the imperfect middle ‘they feasted’, with the ending elided. ἐδεύετο is the imperfect of δεύομαι ‘lack’, taking the genitive δαιτὸς ἐΐσης, ‘the equally shared feast’, and θυμός is ‘heart’. οὐδέ τι is ‘and not at all’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
κοίτου τε μνήσαντο καὶ ὕπνου δῶρον ἕλοντο.
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
of rest they thought and of sleep took the gift.
sentences.i: But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, they thought of rest and took the gift of sleep.
sentences.n: The first line is the formula for the end of a meal, αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο, which stands elsewhere in the poem and keeps its English: ἐξ … ἕντο is a tmesis of ἐξίημι ‘send out’, so they ‘put away’ the desire for drink and food, both genitives. κοίτου τε μνήσαντο is ‘and they thought of rest’, μιμνήσκομαι taking the genitive, and ὕπνου δῶρον ἕλοντο is ‘and took the gift of sleep’, ἕλοντο being the aorist middle of αἱρέω ‘take’.
